Author: @joebyvictor
Content:
Great insights as usual, thanks Marques! I genuinely think this is all about price point and accessibility. For anyone who's done an Apple Vision Pro demo in the Apple Store, they will know how insane and potentially game changing it could be for everyone. The fact is people aren't going to drop $3500 for a supplementary (or what they see as supplementary) product. People still need their phones and their laptops/iPads, so this isn't a primary device, at least not in the current iteration, so not being able to squeeze AVP into people's tech budget cannot be underestimated as a barrier..

The high price point has also means most people haven't actually tried AVP themselves, and as someone who thought it was cool whilst watching all of the initial videos and hype, I couldn't prepare myself for just how blown away I was when I finally tried it last month for the first time, I remember thinking "I NEED to have this in my life!" So the magic of this device ONLY comes with trying it, and most people won't - again because of the price.


I don't see AR glasses in the same category, they're much more practical and allow us to do everyday tasks more efficiently and simultaneously. Whilst they do and will offer some really neat features, it's a completely different product line and it's not about immersion it's about utility and accessibility, but they definitely have wider everyday appeal. It's for this reason that I believe Apple Vision Pro will still have it's viral moment, Apple will unveil a cheaper more comfortable accessible version or Vision Pro with arguably even more functionality, it's just a matter of when not if.

It definitely feels like Apple is trying to get ahead of the curve or at least, be in the race with AR glasses. I think it's a smart decision, but I do wish they hadn't dropped development of AVP. If any company could resource multiple high-end products – Apple can! But I think it's a decision resulting from the market moving at such a rapid pace, and with all of the issues with Apple Intelligence and failures of internal resources, they're being more focused and cautious with future projects, which is sensible, and whilst disappointing for AVP, I think it means we will get a REALLY good AR glass product as a result.

I'm confident Apple will return to AVP once glasses are up and walking. 

In the mean time I will be getting the AVP soon and cannot wait! EDIT - I work in AV in my day job and I'm a video editor so I get that my reaction to and use case of AVP is going to be pumped up compared tp most regular tech users. For me, those little incremental upgrades have tipped the scales and I've been saving!

Author: @Gaurav-bu5be
Content:
🧠 Summary
Apple’s second-generation Vision Pro headset gets a modest upgrade: the new M5 chip and a redesigned Dual Knit Band. While performance improves slightly, the core hardware remains unchanged—same cameras, displays, frame, and weight. The real story? Apple seems to be quietly pivoting away from headsets toward smart glasses, acknowledging that the Vision Pro hasn’t become the mainstream hit they hoped for.

🔍 Highlights
0:20 M5 Chip Arrives

Apple introduces the base M5 chip in Vision Pro, iPad Pro, and 14" MacBook Pro.

No M5 Pro/Max yet; high-end devices like Mac Studio still on older chips.

1:51 Hardware: Mostly the Same

Vision Pro retains same frame, sensors, displays, and battery.

No weight reduction; in fact, it’s slightly heavier due to the new band.

3:09 Dual Knit Band Upgrade

Replaces the uncomfortable Solo Knit Band.

Adds tungsten counterweights and adjustable dials for better comfort.

Available separately for $99.

4:52 Performance Gains

Faster app loading, better rendering, and ~20% longer battery life.

Minor visual improvements (e.g., 120Hz refresh vs. 100Hz).

Most users won’t notice the difference.

6:36 Market Shift & Competition

Samsung launches its own XR headset (“Project Moohan”) with Android XR.

Few other companies are competing in high-end headset space.

7:44 Smart Glasses Rising

Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses show faster innovation and broader appeal.

Lower social penalty makes them more wearable in public.

9:14 Apple’s Strategic Pivot

Vision Pro mostly used for movies and gathers dust.

Apple reportedly cancels lighter “Vision Pro Air” and shifts focus to smart glasses.

Reflects broader industry trend: trimming down headsets vs. building up glasses.

Author: @WAATANG
Content:
I have one and think it’s the best piece of tech I’ve ever had. The capability of the headset itself is amazing. For me the absolute best use of the headset is one which the rest of the world isn’t setup for yet and apple haven’t pushed (but strangely is their biggest marketing/selling point on phones) - personal home photos and videos but in VR180 (if you don’t know what that is, look it up!) I have a dual lens camera which is homemade but canon do sell one at an eyewatering price. It takes dual 180 degree 16k photos and video which you can import onto the headset and literally rewatch in insane quality on the vision pro display. It’s like you’re looking through your eyes again in 3 dimensional viewing and at the correct scale (which is something you don’t realise current viewing of media doesn’t do, it has a huge impact in the reality of it). It’s the real deal and is unbelievable, it’s truly the future and is already here but it’s not accessible and not widely known about. When i show my friends the VR180 photos they all have no idea it existed and they are blown away by it. I bought the vision pro and VR180 camera upon the birth of my daughter and we can put the headset on and look at her aged 1 day old in the exact same way! It makes traditional photos seem like the stone age. The vision pro itself does take a small 3d picture but it’s nothing compared to VR180.

Unfortunately as vision pro is so expensive there is a small number of people who have them. This combined with a misplaced negative opinion about what it does mainly fuelled by its price, means it has not received the investment from developers that it needs. It’s a different offering to quest 3, those who compare them like the old playstation vs xbox argument are completely missing the point. I do understand their frustration. If it was more accessible to the masses the future development of this product line would change the world like it should be. Instead, for most people it’s only useful for watching films on (viewing quality on vision pro is the best you’ll see) The Apple VR180 documentaries and ringside sports viewing are unreal, my grandad gets to see elephants again like he’s there again in his youth when he could travel, he cried when he saw this. The few apps which did get development are amazing. Due to this slow uptake and this stagnant innovation from apple, it’s clear that it’s before it’s time. I have no doubt this will be the future. I am sad to see that the innovation is not as fast as I want it to be and the camera market is non existent. I am so glad they made it available so I already get to make use of that future, when I’m old I will one of few people my age who can look back and relive memories of my family and my daughter growing up.

Author: @VAF84
Content:
I went down the rabbit hole trying to find the right productivity headset that would allow me to untether me from the desk. Eventually I realized these immersive “goggles” weren’t it. I ended up with XReal glasses. In reality, I need something that allows me to work inconspicuously, as if I have a big monitor; when sitting outside on a picnic table, flying, or generally trying to work away from my desk. 

The downside has been that because it needs to be connected via USB, our corporate security software shuts down data when it senses the USB plugged in. The workaround requires that I plug an hdmi in to the computer, plug XReal usb into output plug of hdmi adapter,the power usb into said adapter and into the laptop with a data blocker adapter. Someone needs to make a set of glasses with the proper pixels to present the augmented reality monitor in a large size, wirelessly. Interaction with the augmented reality is a bonus. XReal is pretty close.

Content: I have an Apple Vision Pro M2 and even though I overall don't regret purchasing it, I really just have no good reason to spend another nearly $5K on an Apple Vision Pro M5. Yes, that is what my AVPM2 cost after getting the 1TB storage, plus AppleCare, plus taxes, around $4800 as I recall. I sorta had the "Fields Of Dreams" mentality when it came to the AVPM2 meaning "if you build it, they (developers) will come".  Except the gaming developers for the most part never showed up. Honestly, as fantastic graphically, as the AVPM2 appears, is it even capable of playing the plethora of VR games that you see on the Meta Quest 3, if developers chose to port any of those games over??  Like Metro Awakening VR, Alien Rogue Incursion VR, Behemoth VR, etc.  I have never seen any evidence in the AVPM2 that it is even capable of a 1st Person Shooter game thus far.  That has always been where my disappointment has been meaning there are not a lot of actual VR games.  I always felt that if Apple had truly worked with VR developers and had launched with 20+ actual great VR games that it would have been way more successful.  As it is, we keep getting these AR games that, in my opinion, don't have long term appeal. Anyway, been supporting Apple for many decades, and keep hoping for more VR gaming support from developers. Author: @RahulAg-e5q
Content:
Apple should rethink the design of Vision Pro. Instead of building a full computer inside the headset, they can keep only the display system, sensors, and the R1 chip for camera processing and calibration, and remove the main CPU and heavy processing hardware from the headset. The battery can be built inside the Vision Pro for convenience, and the external pack can become an optional CPU module.

Then the Vision Pro could connect through Type-C or Thunderbolt to an iPhone, iPad, or Mac, and use the processing power of that device. That way, if someone already has a powerful MacBook or iPhone, they don’t need to pay again for a second CPU inside the headset. They just connect it and instantly get full performance with zero lag through Thunderbolt.

For people who want to use the Vision Pro as a standalone computer, Apple could sell the external CPU module separately, similar to the current battery pack but with actual processing hardware inside it. This would make the Vision Pro more modular, more affordable, and more flexible.

Author: @WelcometotheMuseum
Content:
As a museum worker I would love to see more of these in the museums. It is a great tool and I’ve already seen some of them in the exhibition halls (not Apple though, other more affordable VR sets). It is really helpful to visualize the scene from the past or to show the reconstruction of the destroyed place. I was working once on the 3D scanning of the heritage site so the students in another country could “visit” it with the Quest 3. That was absolutely amazing, I am sure with the Apple Silicone it would be even better. The problem is that the museums and cultural institutions rarely have money for that 😅 and Apple would never sponsor such projects I assume. 
Another problem with the shared use of VR sets is that you have to quickly clean it somehow, so it means somebody has to build a special device for that specific purpose. Or they should develop yet another, more practical strap made of plastic or something, so it can be easily wiped 😅

These comments always show proof of people speaking with nothing to say. Everyone wants to be a critic these days with nothing but a negative bias on “new = bad”

Many people form strong opinions about technology based on what they think they know, failing to recognize the realistic timeline and significance of how innovations evolve.

Author: @ktkthakre
Content:
I think the glasses win here. Because:
- Convenience: You can just put them on and boom, you are in. There's not much hassle to it. People with glasses are already doing the same thing everyday; take them out of the case, put them on and they go about their routine. The glasses doesn't hamper your routine.
- Price: Glasses will be widely used and will have a lower price tag.
- Non-full Immersion: People will appreciate if immersion is not full, at least for the average consumer. If you are working and people often need your attention then glasses do not compromise it, where as the the VR/AR headsets needs you to remove them or pause/stop whatever you are doing to give your full attention to someone.

The headsets only win in one category: Full immersion. Other than that, it not convenient, its not pocket friendly and it obstructs your senses, not to remind you, the screens are literally 2 centimeters from your eyes which causes you screen fatigue which isn't great for in the long run.

However, it's really an engineering marvel to have these products exist the way they do.

Content:
Quick thought MB:  maybe if we extrapolate Vision Pro and Meta Ray-ban Display into Apple past we can know where they are going.

So Vision Pro and Meta Quest are kinda like the Apple Lisa and the Xerox Star, maybe not in that order, but you get the drill.  A grandeur imagineering of what's coming but not really the exact vision people want.  Larry Tesler which invented the Alto, helped on the Star and took full ownership of the Lisa was more famous for the invention of copy-paste and WYSIWYG didn't quite got it even after 3 different approaches.  So this might be the case with the VR headsets, the form factor might be all wrong and the interface might be a little off.

But the Meta Ray-Ban Display might be the Apple Macintosh which was a proto laptop just with a CRT and a detachable keyboard.  Today we know those two were a mistake and that people wanted an integrated system (like the Amiga 1200) but that also included an LCD display and a trackpad, just like the First PowerBooks.

Meta's greatest achievement it's the Meta Neural Band but they need more to advance that device. Eventually they could invent the VGA of Smart Glasses, but they need to think outside of their box and stop forcing only Meta only apps there.

Author: @ramkumarrealm
Content:
“What’s Going on with Apple Vision Pro?”:

Apple Vision Pro 2 (2025): The second-gen Vision Pro headset keeps the same design, displays, sensors, and core features as the original but upgrades the processor from M2 to the new M5 chip.

What’s New: The main upgrade is a redesigned, much more comfortable dual-knit band, which distributes the weight better—but actually results in a slightly heavier device. You can also buy this new band separately for the original Vision Pro.

Performance: The M5 chip brings faster app loading, a minor increase in rendered pixels, and about 20% more battery life. But these are small improvements—most everyday users won’t notice dramatic differences.

Software: All Vision Pros now get new visionOS 26 features, including better personas, pinnable widgets, and converting photos into spatial scenes.

No Major Redesign: The core complaints from the first version (heaviness, comfort) persist except for the improved band. Cameras, displays, and general form factor are unchanged.

Market Context: Samsung has entered the market with its Android XR headset, but otherwise, few companies are releasing direct Vision Pro competitors. Meanwhile, the smart glasses category (like Meta Ray-Bans) is advancing rapidly and becoming more appealing to regular users.

Apple’s Strategic Shift: Usage data shows most people use Vision Pro mainly for movies, and many units are gathering dust. Apple appears to be scaling back ambition—reportedly canceling lighter Vision Pro versions and shifting focus to smart glasses, where social acceptance and utility are higher.

Industry Trend: Tech firms are attacking “mixed reality” from two directions: big, powerful headsets like Vision Pro (trimming them down) or smart glasses (building them up). The latter approach is gaining real-world traction.

Bottom line: The Vision Pro 2 offers modest technical improvements. The industry is watching whether XR headsets or lightweight smart glasses will win the future of “face computers”—for now, more people prefer smart glasses for everyday use.

Author: @five-toedslothbear
Content:
Thanks for the video. It’s been a 7 hour Vision Pro day for me so far, and I’m planning to upgrade from the M2 to M5 model. I think there’s room for both types of headsets. I don’t think I’d ever use smart glasses: I’d need _prescription_ smart glasses with _another_ set of $300 lenses in them, and now I wear both progressives and bifocal computer glasses, so two sets of smart glasses to go with my two sets of dumb glasses? Smart glasses good, but I’m probably not the audience.

But, I’m comfortable for hours in the Vision Pro, the fixed focal distance works well with my presbyopia. 

I think it’s a good move. The current Vision Pro is insanely great tech that needs more content and apps. Besides the chip upgrade, I don’t think there’s any room to spec anything else up.

Apple can make some smart glasses, which they should do, and once that happens, the start of the art for immersive wear will move, and they can work on better, faster, lighter immersive kit. I think there is a market for both form factors, just like there’s a market for tablet and laptop. That’s my take.

Author: @Spinelli__
Content: For anyone who wants at least as good, if not better, quality optics, FOV, etc. as the Apple Vision Pro but just want to use pure VR (not MR/AR stuff) than I highly, highly recommend checking out the Pimax Dream Air. The Pimax Dream Air comes with an updated version of the Sony Micro-OLED panels in the AVP while delivering 110 to 115-ish degrees H.FOV and around 100 degrees stereo overlap - the largest h.FOV of any OLED headset in the market and one of the largest, if not the largest, stereo overlap of any headset. For comparison, the AVP's h.FOV is only around 100 and has poor-to-average stereo/binocular overlap of around 80 degrees. Weight-wise, the Dream Air weighs under 170 g (under 0.37 lbs) compared to the Vision Pro's 650 to 800 grams (1.43 to 1.76 lbs) excluding battery. The Pimax does all that while costing only 36% to 46% of the Apple at 2000 to 2300 USD VS the AVP's 5000 to 5600 USD.

Author: @BennettMeierWerks
Content:
The fact that I can’t walk into an Apple Store and buy everything I need for my business and family — while ensuring everyone’s on the same “M” performance generation — is so frustrating. Why can I buy an iPad with an M5, a MacBook Pro with an M4 Max, a Mac Studio with an M3 Ultra, an iMac with an M4, and a Mac mini with an M4 Pro? It feels like every product in Apple’s lineup is on a completely different release cycle, sometimes years apart.

I remember when you could walk into an Apple Store and buy an iMac, a MacBook, a MacBook Pro, and a Mac Pro — and they were all on the same generation of hardware. You knew that when you made that purchase, you were getting the most up-to-date machine available. Now it just feels like an enormous compromise if you want a different form factor. I’d love to have an M5 Max iMac, but that’s clearly not happening, so I have to settle for the MacBook Pro. As a consumer, I might have bought both — but I don’t want to buy a computer that’s outdated the day I purchase it.

Author: @charliekempf
Content:
I think the main problem with the vision pro is the software ecosystem. Apple is pitching this like a wearable computer (with specs to match) but the software model is like the iPhone and iPad. The benefit of a Mac Is that you can develop software on a Mac, compile on a Mac, then run that software without needing to get app store approval, pay a cut to apple etc. This allows developers to easily play around with the hardware and make compelling software (which you *need* to move units). The apple vision pro is a marvelous piece of hardware with no compelling apps! 

I am an aerospace engineer and if I can do parametric CAD on this thing I would pick it up in 2 seconds, but that isn't going to happen if the software distribution model is like an iPad. And if the only things you can run on this thing are glorified iPhone apps, its no wonder they are losing out to cheaper smart glasses which can also run smartphone apps. This is a PC level piece of hardware which needs PC level software support in order to succeed

Content: Nothing changed on purpose so that companies who are developing sdks and applications for the Apple Vision Pro don’t have to throw out half of their effort. I’m not choosing the Apple Vision Pro because it’s best but rather because those other devices will be discontinued soon. The executives at Apple need as little reason as possible to pull the plug on this project, because it is an incredibly difficult market to find success in when you consider that in the 10 years since the first marketable MR device was released (Microsoft HoloLens 1), every single MR device released has lost the company and investors billions of dollars. Forget commercial success, none have yet proven themselves to be anything other than a massive waste of time and resources. Apple is being smart by extending the lifetime of the platform to allow enough time for the market to stabilize around it.

Author: @xPir8x
Content: Having just watched the Tested review of the M5 version of Vision Pro, it's interesting to hear the differences between folks that use the VP near daily and folks like yourself that are a lot more novelty/casual use. Neither are wrong and both make good points, but the interesting thing is there's indepth review from folks that are all in and then there's yeah, but let's look at Vision Pro vs whoever else is making something similar (note: MAN...could that Samsung look more like a knock-off in both hardware and software? Damn.) I'm nowhere near one of those Apple-can-do-no-wrong fanboys, but I'm taking the Vision Pro from the perspective that it's emerging tech and Apple hasn't abandoned it just because the numbers weren't what might have been expected. I like everything you had to say, except for 2 things: we all need to stop emphasizing the price tag. Macbooks, Mini Studio, Mac Pro...none of it is cheap, so why are we laboring over the price of the Vision Pro? Well, because it's seen as a non-essential, luxury niche item and WHOA it's SOOO EXPENSIVE! But for what the tech is, it's really not. Hell, my Powerbook 1400 was over $3k back in the late 90s. The second thing is when has Apple ever had a product that was a straight up, smash hit, clearing the shelves at introduction? Pretty much never. Apple has always wanted to be that, but the reality is that they are more of a slow burn company. Their tech is a slow tide and it eventually catches on and many others make knock offs along the way which only shows off how good the original products are. Yes, other companies are making stuff and they are making it cheaper. If those are the priorities, have at it. Everyone should buy what they want and if that's glasses instead of a headset, have at it. Who cares? I know the Vision Pro isn't for everyone, currently, but it's no Newton. It's not going away. Unless you think about now the iPhone was just the next version of the Newton and the Newton never really went away! Ha! Anyway, solid stuff and nice review, man! Thanks so much for all your work!

Author: @lc9245
Content: I have thought about these for a while. I'm still of the opinion that these devices should be an accessory, an extension of a smartphone than trying to replace it, kind of like smart watch. Those haven't really caught on because they are still just a smartphone, but we have not been able to squeeze smartphone functionalities into smart watch and that's understandable, even desirable I would argue. This suggests that the smart glass should act more like a smart display. With better wireless communication technologies like 5G or Wifi7, I feel it's reaching the point where with a bit of tricks and optimisation; we can offload much of the processing somewhere else like a phone and the smart glass can act as display, interface and data gathering point for them. Trying to do too much on those glasses would be a mistake. Even Meta's implementation feels as if it's trying to do too much on very limited real estate. Much better to leave the heavy lifting somewhere else and do the things that others suck at. If anything, the most exciting thing about Meta implementation is the wrist band thing. Make that work and interface with smart glass will be realised.

Author: @carltonascarf7694
Content:
You touched on the social aspect as a reason people aren't wanting to use the vision pro, and specifically you talked about it seeming 'nerdy'.
I absolutely agree with that, but I think there is a deeper issue at play.

Technology is cool and using better technology is almost always even cooler. But even as we get more advanced with all this, there's still an innate human lust for nature, friends, family - in short, real life. 

When COVID restrictions were easing, people didn't stay indoors and stay on Zoom. We wanted to get out and live our lives again. Experiencing other people is always at the heart of what humans find truly enjoyable.

Products like the vision pro are extremely isolating and take you away from reality, rather than enhancing it. Now inevitably more and more people will buy them and so maybe this will change as and when they become mainstream and easier to wear etc, but I really feel that humanity does have a ceiling to how much we want technology in our lives.

However much it might be difficult and tricky at times, experiencing reality with the people we love is still the best thing that we have, however cringey that may sound.

Author: @onlypaper123
Content:
Vision Pro and Meta glasses are not the starting point for developments toward the same goal.  However, I am sure that both will contribute to the development of future products that lie somewhere in between.
Meta glasses are designed to be worn in any situation and anywhere (so that Meta can access data everywhere and ultimately make money from it). Vision Pro is the situation. Just because it has a battery doesn't mean you have to walk around with it on the street. Why would you? It's obviously designed for immersive entertainment, work, etc. in VR and AR. You put it on when you need it and take it off when you're done. Smart glasses, on the other hand, are designed to provide access to the digital world anytime, anywhere. It's more like a purpose-built tool versus a permanent digital connection.

Content:
I have the Meta Quest 3, and to be honest, they’re pretty much useless. The main reason I bought them was to connect to my PC and use them for flight simulation in VR — and that’s literally their only decent use. You can’t store movies, there aren’t any real games, Game Pass has terrible lag, and the battery at 90 Hz lasts barely half an hour.

There just aren’t any good apps. When I tried the Vision Pro, at least it had a ton more applications — and you can actually use it like a Mac. But it’s not portable, it costs a crazy amount of money… way more than buying a good gaming laptop or a MacBook Pro.

In my country (Mexico), $3,500 USD is literally the price of a used car. To make things worse, I almost bought the Vision Pro two months ago — I was so close — and thank God I didn’t, because I would’ve had a heart attack finding out that just two months later they released the new M5 version out of nowhere.

I think it’s not that popular yet because people still don’t really know what it’s for — and because it’s way too expensive. But it’s easily a thousand times better than the Meta Quest. I just wish it could connect to a PC — if that were possible, I would’ve bought it a long time ago.

3:44 you’d think that they’d learn to put the head straps on the first design of the Vision Pros, specially since the first Quest came out in 2019. But I guess this is apples way of improving on things, by being late to the party by 5 years.

Content: Great review,  Honestly I am not a fan of comparing the smart glasses to HMDs. Author: @PortRhouse
Content:
I think the VR/XR space has been moving towards the "smart glasses" form factor because companies have just failed to realize the biggest use case for more immersive VR. Immersive VR is not just a smartphone on your face with a fancy HUD like smart glasses are. Sure, it could act as a productivity tool like a phone or laptop, but Immersive VR is primarily a social and entertainment platform. I want to be able to build a whole virtual world for myself not constrained by real world limitations like expensive furniture, real estate, or even the laws of physics. I want to be able to create a highly customizable avatar to represent myself that could be genuinely anything humanoid. Not just a generic metahuman. 

People could invite their friends who live far away to hang out in their world, watch TV, play games, or explore other worlds together. It could enable socialization thousands of miles away. It could transcend language barriers. It could give disabled people the ability to walk, hell even fly if they wanted to. It could enable trans or genderfluid people to inhabit a body they actually feel comfortable in when they look in the mirror. It could enable people to experience the wonders of the world when travel is financially out of reach. VRchat may be old, niche, and get a bad reputation. However, it is the perfect example of a VR application with a VERY dedicated, growing, creative userbase. If a social platform like that could be created for a mainstream audience and made available through an easy to use, high quality headset I guarantee you it would take off. You cannot tell me that would not be a smash hit that moves units. Its ability to double as a productivity device would just be a bonus.

Author: @djrt8179
Content:
I spent years trying to tell people full on VR isn't the future. But they kept pointing to TV and Movies showing how amazing and incredible it could be. They had this idea in their head based on a fake reality that they were building their decisions off of. Full on VR was NEVER the answer. Ever. It is a novelty. Always has been. There's 3 things a new product needs to do at least 2 of to gain adoption. It needs to be more efficient, it needs to replace something we already do and be better than the current version, and it needs to be easy to learn/get involved.

Is VR more efficient? No, you need to tailor everything around the headset like space, trusting the people around you not to mess with you, and making sure everything in your vicinity is basically blind person proof. Is it better than what we currently have? In some ways sure, but a lot of people prefer just gaming on a tv or multi tasking with an iPad and phone. And is it easy to get involved? No, you can't pick up and play, it's a whole extra investment for something not that intuitive, it's not that simple.

VR was NEVER the future and I'm so glad people have stopped pretending they're going to live in an Apple VR headset.

Author: @tomwilko7841
Content: Not tried the smart glasses but a buddy has the apple vr and whilst it's extra difficult for me as a spectacles wearer (the design certainly isn't catered to that particular cohort) at first it is an amazing experience....but it soon becomes tiresome, the os is not easily learned by non enthusiasts and there are no compelling games or experiences as yet, I was always happy my turn was over and couldn't wait to get the contraption off my head....my buddy was an early occulus investor so I've had the experience of seeing vr develop as a non-enthusiast and from my particular perspective they are still way way off from having a useful product...i don't know if it's the weight or just the vr experiences effect on my body but every single time I've had a headset on, from the first occulus to the apple device, after about 10 minutes l get this raised area, about a cm in width, starting above one ear, circling the back of my head and finishing at my other ear....i think it's a vein (tho it genuinely feels much more solid than a typical vein, there is zero sponginess in it's texture) that is otherwise never called into action during my normal life, and it feels like it's constricting my head, it's not painful but it's most definitely uncomfortable and it comes as a blessed relief to take the headset off, I've often wondered if it's something to do with my eyesight as I'm very short sighted and often have had to remove my glasses to fit into the set, then again I've thought it might be a side effect of my senses struggling to adapt to vr or like I say it could just be the weight on my head for an extended time causing it, I don't suffer from migraines but from what I've read about them it sounds a little like one of the symptoms....anyways I seriously doubt these things will take off until they can solve this problem because if its happening to me it's undoubtedly happening to many others and if it is something to do with sensory overload they have a serious problem

Marques, here’s a real world review on an almost daily use case from an owner. I do have some caveats.
- I love Apple products
- I own a couple tech companies
- been doing VR for over 14 years

OK with that out of the way on a scale of one to 10 based on the competition, I feel that the Apple Vision Pro gets a solid 8… in its current form. I believe it or not. I believe the only way to get it to a 10 (it pains me to say this) is if another company made the software.

I’m gonna be straight up Apple did some great things with the Vision Pro. But just like with iOS, Apple’s gonna tell you what they’re gonna do. For example, we don’t get videos on our lock screens. Why? Because Apple has to protect us from ourselves and battery usage instead of giving us the choice. Can we put the icons anywhere? No, they have to be in a grid. Stuff like this drives me nuts about Apple but there’s a new one for the Apple Vision Pro… native, and snake oil 😬.

Apple gives us the ability to install all iOS and iPadOS apps on our vision pros… but the fine print is the developer has to opt in. So yes, on a plane I can watch anything from Disney+. But the content that I consume daily is on YouTube. Google opted it out so we can’t even put the iPad app on the Vision Pro. Why does this matter? I pay for YouTube so I would like to have downloaded items ready. What’s my work around? Download them on my iPad and share my iPad screen to my headset. Ugh. This is a major pain because I can’t do this with Netflix either.  

And then comes the native apps. Come on Apple! A killer app would be going through Apple Maps in complete VR!! how do I know this? Because if you’ve never used Google Earth 14 years ago on the oculus rift, you have no idea what you’re missing. I think Google made the perfect app and I am not a fan of Google at all. You could legitimately grab the sun and move the sun around the Earth and change how things look in real time. You can fly in from orbit and zoom all the way down to street view. This was a phenomenal way of using the Maps. And I think Apple Maps is better so the Fidelity would be better plus we’re using much more powerful chips. But calendar, maps, numbers, etc. are all iPadOS apps. Sure at least they checked the check box to make sure it can be installed on the Apple Vision Pro, but damn I really wish it was native. And immersive. 

I use my headset approximately 5 to 7 hours a day for work. I work mobile so I don’t have the luxury of having a really bad ass home set up. But when I’m on the road, I whip out my laptop and have a massive screen. I don’t go with the Ultra Wide but I do go with the wide screen and that’s perfect for anything that I need to do on my laptop. However, I wish I didn’t have to take out my laptop. I wish I could have the experience from my laptop inside the headset because I have more space to work with.  

Now it sounds like Samsung’s product will work with all mobile apps. I can’t stress enough how amazing this is. For example, gaming. I have some iPadOS games that are installed in the headset and all I have to do is turn on my headset and take my PlayStation five controller and now I’m gaming. However, Fortnite is now available for the iPadOS…. But I can’t play it in the headset so what do I do? Loaded up on my iPad and share my iPad screen. Totally unnecessary, but it works. What about Call of Duty®? Talk about an amazing experience inside the headset. But the developer opted out. It seems like Samsung won’t have this issue. People have no idea until it hits the market how amazing the Samsung product is going to be for gaming. Now imagine once these headsets start having PlayStation five level chips inside of them…. You literally have a console on your face where you can play in 8K pretty much anywhere. And don’t even get me started on the Apple Intelligence versus Google’s or anybody else’s. I feel like Apple’s product had a two year on the market head start, and is gonna lose it immediately. 

Do I watch movies on my headset? Every now and then, but I consume more YouTube than any other media. 

Sidenote, I picked up another headset from my wife, and when I’m out of town, we still watch our shows together just remotely on the headset and she loves it… but after a couple, our long shows, she is done with the weight of the headset. I don’t notice it because I guess since I’ve been doing it for 14 years, I developed the muscle muscles that are needed to not feel the weight. I don’t know. I’ve never had issues with weight from headsets and I’ve owned every quest and every rift on my way to the Apple Vision Pro.

But anyway, that’s my honest review, and I’m a fanboy. Lol. I might pick up the other strap, but as of right now I feel like Apple’s dropping the ball on the software. But I still give it a solid eight out of 10 for experience I wanted to rate and lower, but I felt like that’s not accurate. That’s just my emotion. lol. I don’t know if you read these but let me know what you think.

Author: @QuentinAnthonyAnderson
Content: I'm confused by the lack of progress on the headset front. I mean, I get the social stigma stuff (and that's real - I've brought my Quest on the last couple flights I've taken and the flights have been so packed, I just didn't feel comfortable pulling it out). But the capabilities these headsets have should be making developers salivate. Everyone knows the holy grail of VR is essentially to create Westworld. If they accomplish that, it would literally be the biggest social advancement since AT LEAST social media, if not ever. But it feels like even knowing that, development is still contingent on people embracing VR wholesale in the interim and that feels like a foolish strategy. Most adults aren't gamers, so expecting them to adopt what right now is essentially gaming technology before the more mainstream offerings are available is unrealistic. I know plenty of people who would love to enter The Matrix but aren't going to prime themselves with Gorilla Tag or Beat Saber for a couple years while what they want is being developed. I think this tech is one of the few examples where you need to build it out FIRST and then the market will respond. I get that that's risky but I feel like this is as sure a bet as it gets, just knowing human tendencies. People will WANT to go to different realities, be whoever they want to be, and interact with interesting people.

Content:
I tried the Vision Pro in the Apple Store and thought it was incredible. But at the same time I have no idea what I’d actually use it for in its current state. If I was wealthy I’d certainly buy one just to play with though. 

I still believe the potential is huge but making that a reality is quite different. 

For example: 

- watching a live sport event as if you’re in the stadium. And sat eight next to your friends with photorealistic avatars
- maybe going to historical sites like the colosseum in Rome, but when wearing it everyone walking past looks like they’re in Roman times and you can go and watch an event as it would have been originally. 
- just being able to hang out with friends rather than a video call. 

I know for some of these types of things people will say it sounds very sad to not have actual in person interaction but be seeing your friends they if h a virtual world. I agree if that’s all you do. But also for people who live busy lives and live far away from their family and friends it could be such an amazing experience. 

It just still even now feels very far away. Having photorealistic avatars is possible now but not realistic for the masses, and of course these headsets are extremely expensive for most people. 

But I do think the potential is huge especially for live entertainment that you’d watch on tv/video instead such as concerts, sport etc. or even just watching movies. 

I do wonder how this kind of tech will go over the next 10-20 years, but I do think we are minimum 10 years away from the kinds of thing I said being widely adopted.

Content: I want to see something that is in-between the smart glasses and the AR headsets come out. Funnily enough, right now it seems like the larger AR headsets are happy with at least a battery in your pocket (we could probably do with some compute components in there and then a clip for your waistband so it can still dissipate heat to lighten up the headset), and the smart glasses try to cram everything into the glasses. This just ends up making the glasses look super clunky. Why not have all of the compute and battery for the smart glasses in something you can put in your pocket and just a magnetic connector that can snap onto either arm? This would enable the glasses to look much more normal when you don't care about using the smart features. Also, I think smart glasses need to ditch the speakers. Almost everyone has wireless earbuds. Save the space and keep the arms nice and thin and cut the speakers out.

Author: @JoeSanta
Content:
If Apple wants Vision Pro to evolve toward a Ray-Ban Meta form factor, they need to rethink the system architecture. Right now everything—compute, sensors, displays, power, cooling—is packed into the headset. Instead, Apple could split it into two parts: lightweight glasses for displays and cameras, plus a pocket or belt-mounted compute/power module (or leverage the iPhone). A dedicated ultra-low-latency wireless link, something in the 60 GHz+ range, could stream high-bandwidth video both ways with predictive buffering to mask any delay.

That would drop face weight, heat, and bulk while keeping performance. It also makes the platform modular: swap the compute pack every few years, keep the glasses. It won’t reach true “sunglass” scale until micro-LED waveguides, compact eye-tracking, and dense batteries mature—but this hybrid setup is the only practical path to getting Vision closer to that Ray-Ban-level comfort

Content: They are two completely different products: the smart glasses and something like the Vision Pro. I don't know why people try to use Vision Pro in public... They will never be the same, and they shouldn't be, even if there's a small number of people who can do their work with both anyway.

Content:
You can't compare smart glasses to vision pro. They're literally polar opposites. AVP is for Immersion. Smart glasses are for day to day utiltiy , like a smart watch, just on your face. 

You can't watch a 4K HDR movie on a smart glasses like you can on AVP. You cant do proper / immersed work on smart glasses like AVP. You can't run demanding 3D Apps like AVP. Etc. etc. etc.

2 totally different markets/use cases. 

Now, AVP can always get slimmer, lighter and cheaper. Even so, even if they made it 30% lighter, 50% price drop ($1.5K) - there is no denying that more people will prob want to buy a $1K pair of smart glasses from Apple vs AVP. Just because of the look/feel and comfort alone. I get it. But both markets/products can co exist.
